why: Rxa8 takes the open a-file and trades off Black's active rook; f4 instead loosens the king and lets the rooks trade on Black's terms.
Black threatened gxh4 and e4; dxe5 dealt with the tension, while Bg3 left the bishop to be hit by e4 and the Nd5 pressure.
The Bc1 was the only guard of b2, so moving it away let the queen take the pawn.
Early f3 weakens the king and blocks the knight instead of developing or capturing the d5 pawn with exd5.
dxe4 resolves the central tension; pinning with Bb4 ignored White's exd5 and d4 break.
Nxd5 was threatened; g4 hit the knight with tempo, while fxe5 left the d5 pawn hanging.
Bf5 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6; f5 is an early pawn move that weakens the king.
The g3 pawn was attacked by the knight and undefended, and a5 ignored that and the king race.
Bb4+ first forces matters before dealing with the bishop on d8; Be7 allowed Bxe7 and Bxc7 ideas.
b4 attacks the rook on c5 with tempo and the king move allowed it; Kf4 kept the king active.
The knight on g3 was nearly trapped; Nf5 rescued it while g5 let Bxg3 win it.
White threatened Ng4+ with mate; Rf8 hit the queen, while Kg7 allowed Bc1+ pinning the knight.
The rook on f1 was undefended and Qxf1+ was a threat, which Qf3 ignored.
The queen on d1 was what defended d5, so moving the bishop away left the pawn to fall.
Rg1+ was coming and Bg5 walks into a pin; Kh8 sidestepped it.
